newsitem.title: UK: UK court lets BCCI employees sue for stigma.
newsitem.headline: UK court lets BCCI employees sue for stigma.

text.p: Britain's highest court on Thursday gave former employees of the collapsed Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) a chance to sue for compensation for the stigma of having worked for the fraud-ridden bank.

In a precedent-setting case, two former senior BCCI employees, Raihan Mahmud and Qaiser Malik made claims against BCCI, now acting through liquidator Deloitte & Touche, saying they could not get jobs because of their link to the bank.
They will now be allowed to start their proceedings against BCCI, which collapsed in 1991 with debts of more than $12 billion amid the biggest fraud in banking history.

The judgement by the House of Lords could affect hundreds of former BCCI employees some of whom are making counter claims including a stigma element against claims by the liquidator for the payment of loans made to them by BCCI.
In a recent report to the British government on the progress of the liquidation, Deloitte & Touche said the stigma claims by employees had "hampered the recovery of loans that were made to staff."
The report said there were around 900 employees with loans outstanding that have issued claims against the liquidator who owe a net amount of over 41 million pounds ($67 million).

In his judgment, Lord Steyn sounded a note of caution to those attempting to claim stigma compensation, something that now every claimant will have to do on an individual basis since Thursday's decision was based only on an agreed set of facts.
"It is...improbable that many employees would be able to prove 'stigma compensation'", Stein said.

He added that such claims would face "formidable practical obstacles" to success - "But difficulties of proof cannot alter the legal principles which permit...such claims for financial loss caused by breach of contract being put forward for consideration."

The current cases assumed that BCCI operated in a corrupt and dishonest manner; that Mahmud and Malik were innocent of any involvement; and that they were disadvantaged in the labour market by their link to BCCI after the bank's conduct became widely known.
Lorinda Peasland of law firm Manches & Co, which has acted for the BCCI employees, said some of the employees will be able to get some compensation.
"We are fairly confident that we will be able to recover on behalf of some of the employees," she told Reuters.

In his judgment, Lord Nicholls of Birkenhead rejected the possible claim that the case would lead to a flood of claims against the liquidator of BCCI. This might make the liquidation, which has already taken five years, proceed even more slowly.
"...it could not be right to allow 'floodgates' arguments of this nature to stand in the way of claims which, as a matter of ordinary legal principle, are well founded," Nicholls said.

Peasland said the judgment also had wider implications, especially in the financial sector, in that it had established for the first time that employees may have a claim if their employer damages their future employment prospects.
